maj26-001.question: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, how should a symptomatic patient with a measured LVEF of 45% be classified?
options: HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF)
HF with reduced EF (HFrEF)
HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
HF with improved EF on treatment
commentaires: Incorrect: the HFmrEF category (LVEF 41–49%) was abolished in the 2026 ESC guidelines.
Correct: HFrEF now covers any LVEF < 50% with symptoms or signs of HF.
Incorrect: HFpEF starts at 50% and requires evidence of diastolic dysfunction.
Incorrect: HF with improved EF requires known HFrEF with an increase of at least 10 points to above 40%.
maj26-001.explication: The 2026 ESC guidelines have abolished the heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction phenotype (HFmrEF, 41–49%), introduced in 2016 mainly for trial enrolment purposes. Only two phenotypes remain: HFrEF, with LVEF < 50% and symptoms or signs of HF, and HFpEF, with LVEF ≥ 50% plus structural or functional abnormalities consistent with diastolic dysfunction, supported by natriuretic peptides. The rationale is that patients with an LVEF of 41–49% have pathophysiology and treatment response close to those of HFrEF. HF with improved EF is defined by an absolute increase of at least 10 points to a final LVEF > 40%; treatment must then be continued. Note that device thresholds are unchanged: primary prevention ICD and CRT are still based on an LVEF ≤ 35%.
maj26-001.aRetenir: ESC 2026: only two phenotypes, HFrEF (LVEF < 50%) and HFpEF (≥ 50%); the ICD and CRT thresholds remain at 35%.

maj26-002.question: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, what is the class of recommendation for a primary prevention ICD in a patient in NYHA class II with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, an LVEF of 30% after more than 3 months of optimal medical therapy and a life expectancy > 1 year?
options: Class I, level of evidence A
Class IIa, level of evidence B1
Class IIb, level of evidence C
Class III, level of evidence B1
commentaires: Incorrect: class I (level B1) is reserved for HFrEF of ischaemic aetiology.
Correct: non-ischaemic aetiology, NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 35% after ≥ 3 months of therapy = IIa, B1.
Incorrect: class IIb C applies to the wearable cardioverter-defibrillator as a bridging solution.
Incorrect: class III applies to implantation within 40 days of myocardial infarction or to NYHA IV patients with no further treatment plan.
maj26-002.explication: The 2026 ESC guidelines retain a gradation by aetiology. In ischaemic patients in NYHA class II–III with an LVEF ≤ 35% despite at least 3 months of optimal guideline-directed medical therapy, an ICD is recommended (class I, level B1), except within 40 days of myocardial infarction (class III). In non-ischaemic patients meeting the same criteria, it should be considered (class IIa, level B1), as the benefit is smaller (DANISH), although a meta-analysis found an overall survival benefit. In the new ESC grading system, level B1 corresponds to at least one adequately powered randomised trial. The benefit declines with age and comorbidities (risk of non-sudden death): the decision should be shared and reassessed before each generator replacement (IIa). The wearable cardioverter-defibrillator is only a bridge (IIb).
maj26-002.aRetenir: ESC 2026: primary prevention ICD if LVEF ≤ 35% after ≥ 3 months of therapy; class I if ischaemic, IIa if non-ischaemic.

maj26-003.question: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, in a symptomatic patient in sinus rhythm with an LVEF ≤ 35% on optimal therapy, which situation corresponds to a class IIb indication for CRT?
options: LBBB, QRS duration 160 ms
LBBB, QRS duration 140 ms
Non-LBBB morphology, QRS duration 160 ms
Non-LBBB morphology, QRS duration 140 ms
commentaires: Incorrect: LBBB ≥ 150 ms = class I, level A, the strongest indication.
Incorrect: LBBB 130–149 ms = class IIa (level C).
Incorrect: non-LBBB ≥ 150 ms = class IIa (level C).
Correct: non-LBBB 130–149 ms = class IIb (level C), where the benefit is least certain.
maj26-003.explication: The 2026 ESC guidelines keep the 2021 ESC gradation, still with an LVEF ≤ 35%. LBBB ≥ 150 ms: class I (A). LBBB 130–149 ms and non-LBBB ≥ 150 ms: class IIa. Non-LBBB 130–149 ms: class IIb. QRS < 130 ms without high-grade AV block: class III (A). The levels of evidence for the intermediate indications are now graded C. New: in a patient with LBBB ≥ 150 ms and an LVEF ≤ 35%, medical therapy may be started and CRT planned at the same time (IIb), with the LVEF reassessed before implantation. The document also introduces the concept of "HF associated with a conduction disorder", to be considered when a reduced LVEF is found with a QRS ≥ 130 ms and no other cause.
maj26-003.aRetenir: CRT (LVEF ≤ 35%): LBBB ≥ 150 = I; LBBB 130–149 or non-LBBB ≥ 150 = IIa; non-LBBB 130–149 = IIb; < 130 = III.

maj26-004.question: What position do the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines take on conduction system pacing (His bundle pacing, LBBAP) in patients with HFrEF?
options: Recommended first line instead of CRT
Class IIa after failed LV lead implantation
No recommendation, for lack of outcome trials
Contraindicated (class III) owing to septal risk
commentaires: Incorrect: biventricular CRT remains the only form of resynchronisation graded in the 2026 ESC HF guidelines.
Incorrect: that was the 2021 ESC position for His bundle pacing; the 2026 ESC HF guidelines give no class.
Correct: there is no randomised trial with patient-centred outcomes, so no recommendation is made.
Incorrect: the guidelines do not advise against it; they consider it promising when CRT is difficult.
maj26-004.explication: Section 6.2.3 of the 2026 ESC guidelines notes that conduction system pacing (His bundle or left bundle branch area pacing) aims to engage the Purkinje network to achieve rapid, synchronous LV activation. LBBAP "may be a feasible alternative to CRT when implantation is difficult". However, no randomised trial has assessed its long-term efficacy and safety on patient-centred outcomes in HFrEF, so no recommendation is made. Other documents are more supportive: the 2021 ESC guidelines give His bundle pacing a IIa recommendation after failed LV lead implantation, and the 2023 HRS guideline and the 2025 ESC consensus consider conduction system pacing a reasonable option, particularly as a bailout. This is an area where the documents diverge.
maj26-004.aRetenir: ESC 2026 HF: no recommendation on conduction system pacing (no trial with clinical outcomes).

maj26-005.question: In a patient with HFrEF and high-grade AV block requiring ventricular pacing, what do the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines recommend?
options: RV pacing, then upgrade if the LVEF deteriorates
CRT rather than RV pacing, class I (A)
CRT only if the intrinsic QRS exceeds 150 ms
CRT rather than RV pacing, class IIa (B1)
commentaires: Incorrect: in HFrEF with a high pacing burden, resynchronisation should not wait for deterioration.
Incorrect: that was the class in the 2021 ESC pacing guidelines; the 2026 ESC HF guidelines downgraded it to IIa.
Incorrect: the recommendation applies regardless of intrinsic QRS duration.
Correct: CRT rather than RV pacing, regardless of NYHA class and QRS duration: IIa, level B1.
maj26-005.explication: Near-permanent RV pacing for high-grade AV block produces a deleterious LBBB-type dyssynchrony in a patient whose LV function is already impaired. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines recommend that CRT rather than RV pacing be considered in patients with HFrEF and an indication for ventricular pacing because of high-grade AV block, regardless of NYHA class and QRS duration (class IIa, level B1). The 2021 ESC pacing guidelines had given it class I (A), including in AF. The 2026 document also points out that pacing indications are the same with or without HF. If the pacing burden is high (complete AV block, AF with slow ventricular response), CRT should be considered. Conduction system pacing is not given a class.
maj26-005.aRetenir: HFrEF + high-grade AV block: CRT rather than RV pacing (ESC 2026 HF: IIa B1; ESC 2021: I A).

maj26-006.question: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, which patient profile qualifies for AV junction ablation combined with CRT (new class IIa recommendation)?
options: Highly symptomatic permanent AF, poor rate control, HF admission
Mildly symptomatic paroxysmal AF, normal LVEF, no hospital admission
Recent-onset persistent AF in a candidate for pulmonary vein isolation
Recurrent typical flutter with no symptoms and a preserved LVEF
commentaires: Correct: permanent AF, failed rate control and at least one HF hospitalisation (APAF-CRT).
Incorrect: without major symptoms or HF, nothing justifies making the patient pacemaker-dependent.
Incorrect: recent-onset persistent AF calls first for a rhythm control strategy.
Incorrect: typical flutter is treated with cavotricuspid isthmus ablation.
maj26-006.explication: The 2026 ESC guidelines introduce a specific recommendation (class IIa, level B1): AV junction ablation combined with CRT should be considered in highly symptomatic permanent AF with poor rate control despite medical therapy and at least one HF hospitalisation. The aim is to reduce symptoms, functional limitation, readmissions and mortality. It is based on APAF-CRT, in which this strategy reduced mortality compared with pharmacological rate control, irrespective of LVEF. CRT avoids the dyssynchrony of exclusive RV pacing. The 2025 ESC consensus considers conduction system pacing (preferably LBBAP) a reasonable option in this setting, whatever the LVEF. Anticoagulation must be continued according to the CHA2DS2-VA score.
maj26-006.aRetenir: ESC 2026 HF: AV junction ablation + CRT for poorly controlled permanent AF with an HF hospitalisation (IIa B1).

maj26-007.question: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, which criteria must ALL be met before AF ablation is considered (class IIa, level C) in a patient with symptomatic HFrEF? (select all that apply)
options: A high AF burden on recordings
Continuous persistent AF for less than one year
A clear causal link between AF and HF
Prior failure of at least two antiarrhythmic drugs
An LVEF ≤ 35% with an ICD or CRT-D in place
commentaires: Correct: a high AF burden is the first required criterion.
Correct: beyond one year of continuous persistent AF, the expected benefit is smaller.
Correct: AF must appear to be responsible for the HF or its worsening.
Incorrect: antiarrhythmic drug failure is not required; most of these drugs should in any case be avoided in HFrEF.
Incorrect: this was an inclusion criterion of CASTLE-AF, not a condition of the recommendation.
maj26-007.explication: In the 2026 ESC guidelines, the trials comparing ablation with pharmacological therapy in HFrEF (CASTLE-AF, CASTLE-HTx…) are considered inconclusive for hospitalisation and mortality, even though ablation is better than antiarrhythmic drugs at reducing recurrences. The recommendation for ablation is therefore downgraded to class IIa, level C, in carefully selected patients who meet all three criteria: high AF burden, continuous persistent AF for less than one year and a clear causal link between AF and HF. Data in HFpEF are limited. The 2024 ESC AF guidelines remain more supportive (class I when an arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy is highly likely, IIa in selected HFrEF patients to reduce hospitalisation and mortality): the documents diverge. Finally, propafenone, flecainide and dronedarone should be avoided in HFrEF; amiodarone is the antiarrhythmic drug that can be used.
maj26-007.aRetenir: ESC 2026 HF: AF ablation in HFrEF is IIa C, only with a high burden, persistence < 1 year and clear causality.

maj26-008.question: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, in which patient should remote pulmonary artery pressure monitoring with an implantable sensor be considered (class IIa)?
options: Stable NYHA II HF, no hospitalisation for two years
End-stage NYHA IV HF on inotropes, awaiting transplant
NYHA III HF with an HF hospitalisation within the year
Any CRT-D recipient, regardless of NYHA class
commentaires: Incorrect: stable class II patients do not match the trial populations.
Incorrect: in end-stage HF, the priority is mechanical circulatory support or transplantation.
Correct: NYHA III and an HF hospitalisation within 12 months = IIa, level B1.
Incorrect: the sensor is independent of any cardiac device and targets a specific population.
maj26-008.explication: Of the invasive remote monitoring techniques, only pulmonary artery pressure sensor-guided management (e.g. CardioMEMS) has been evaluated in several randomised trials. CHAMPION, GUIDE-HF and MONITOR-HF showed a reduction in HF hospitalisations in NYHA class III patients hospitalised within the previous year, regardless of LVEF. The 2026 ESC guidelines therefore upgrade it from IIb (2021) to IIa, level B1, in this population. Non-invasive remote monitoring (weight, heart rate, blood pressure) may be considered (IIb). The 2025 HFA consensus stresses the need to optimise therapy and to look for an ICD or CRT indication before implanting the sensor.
maj26-008.aRetenir: Pulmonary artery pressure sensor: NYHA III + HF hospitalisation within 12 months (ESC 2026: IIa B1).

maj26-009.question: True or false: the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines give a class of recommendation to HF monitoring by implanted cardiac devices (thoracic impedance, heart sounds, multiparameter indices such as HeartLogic or TriageHF).
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the guidelines consider the evidence of clinical benefit insufficient and await ongoing trials.
Correct: no recommendation is made; only pulmonary artery pressure monitoring (IIa) and non-invasive remote monitoring (IIb) are graded.
maj26-009.explication: The 2026 ESC guidelines describe the monitoring provided by pacemakers, ICDs and CRT devices: thoracic impedance, heart sounds, respiration, heart rate, arrhythmias and system integrity. It helps to distinguish stable patients from those who need to be seen promptly, and it detects device malfunction and arrhythmias. However, according to the document, there is little evidence that it improves clinical outcomes, and randomised trials are ongoing. No class is therefore given. Only two recommendations exist: pulmonary artery pressure monitoring (IIa B1) and non-invasive remote monitoring (IIb B1). Technical remote monitoring of cardiac devices remains governed by the 2021 ESC guidelines, the 2022 ESC guidelines and the 2023 HRS consensus.
maj26-009.aRetenir: ESC 2026 HF: no recommendation for device-based HF algorithms (OptiVol, HeartLogic, TriageHF), for lack of clinical evidence.

maj26-010.question: A patient with a dual-chamber pacemaker for AV block has 95% RV pacing. He develops HFrEF (LVEF 30%, paced QRS 170 ms) that worsens despite optimal therapy. What do the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines advise?
options: Upgrade from pacemaker to a CRT system
Reprogramming to VVI 40 bpm to limit RV pacing
Adding a single-chamber ICD without changing the pacing
Monitoring alone as long as the LVEF stays above 25%
commentaires: Correct: LVEF ≤ 35%, a high RV pacing burden and worsening HF: a CRT upgrade should be considered (IIa B1, BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade).
Incorrect: in AV block, lowering the rate does not eliminate pacing and exposes the patient to bradycardia.
Incorrect: a single-chamber ICD would leave the dyssynchrony caused by RV pacing unchanged.
Incorrect: there is no 25% threshold; waiting allows HF to progress.
maj26-010.explication: RV pacing can induce HFrEF in some patients (incidence of 5.9 to 39% depending on the definition). The 2026 ESC guidelines recommend checking the RV pacing percentage in any device recipient with new-onset or worsening HFrEF (IIa C). They recommend that an upgrade to CRT be considered in pacemaker or ICD recipients with an LVEF ≤ 35% whose HF worsens despite optimal therapy with a significant proportion of RV pacing (IIa B1). The main supporting evidence is BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade: with ≥ 20% RV pacing and a QRS ≥ 150 ms, upgrading to CRT-D reduced the primary composite endpoint of death, HF hospitalisation and absence of reverse remodelling (HR 0.27). The 2025 ESC consensus also considers an upgrade to conduction system pacing a possible option.
maj26-010.aRetenir: HFrEF in a device recipient: check the RV pacing percentage; if LVEF ≤ 35%, upgrade to CRT (IIa B1).

maj26-011.question: According to the 2026 ESC guidelines on cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease, which statement about ICDs in haemodialysis patients is correct?
options: A primary prevention ICD is recommended if the LVEF is ≥ 35%
A transvenous ICD is preferred as infection risk is not increased
Any ICD is contraindicated, including for secondary prevention
An S-ICD may be considered if no pacing, CRT or ATP is needed
commentaires: Incorrect: the ICD2 trial was neutral; a routine primary prevention ICD is not recommended (class III C) in haemodialysis patients with an LVEF ≥ 35%.
Incorrect: renal failure and dialysis access increase the risk of device infection.
Incorrect: only routine primary prevention is discouraged; an indicated ICD remains an option, with the S-ICD in mind.
Correct: an S-ICD may be considered (IIb C) to limit the risk of device infection.
maj26-011.explication: Sudden cardiac death is a leading cause of death on dialysis, but the randomised ICD2 trial (dialysis patients with an LVEF ≥ 35%) showed no effect of a primary prevention ICD on sudden cardiac death or 5-year mortality. The 2026 ESC guidelines on cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease therefore advise against routine primary prevention ICD implantation in haemodialysis patients with an LVEF ≥ 35% (class III, level C). This does not rule out every ICD: when there is an indication (e.g. secondary prevention), an S-ICD may be considered (IIb C) if there is no need for bradycardia pacing, resynchronisation or ATP, because device infection is more common in these patients. An antibacterial envelope may also be considered (IIb C) in haemodialysis or kidney transplant patients, and the 2021 ESC guidelines suggest a leadless pacemaker as an alternative in haemodialysis patients.
maj26-011.aRetenir: Haemodialysis: no routine primary prevention ICD (ICD2); if an ICD is indicated, consider an S-ICD.

maj26-012.question: According to the 2025 ESC/EHRA consensus statement on indications for conduction system pacing, what is advised when the LV lead cannot be placed via the coronary sinus in a CRT candidate?
options: Abandon resynchronisation and implant a single-chamber ICD
Wait six months, then retry the same coronary venous route
Use conduction system pacing as a bailout strategy
Place the RV lead in a septal position to narrow the QRS
commentaires: Incorrect: the patient still has an indication for resynchronisation, which must be achieved another way.
Incorrect: deferring makes no sense when an effective alternative is available straight away.
Correct: His bundle or left bundle branch area pacing is advised as a bailout.
Incorrect: RV septal pacing does not resynchronise the LV.
maj26-012.explication: The 2025 ESC consensus statement, developed with EHRA input, advises conduction system pacing as a bailout when a coronary sinus lead cannot be implanted. For LBBB with a QRS ≥ 130 ms and an LVEF ≤ 35%, it considers conduction system pacing-based resynchronisation (CSP-CRT) a possible alternative to biventricular CRT. However, its value remains uncertain in the absence of LBBB or with an LVEF > 35%. It also considers it a reasonable option in AV block or AV junction ablation, whatever the LVEF (preferably LBBAP), as well as for upgrades or in non-responders. LBBAP provides better sensing and fewer complications than His bundle pacing. These are consensus statements without classes; the 2026 ESC HF guidelines make no recommendation on this subject.
maj26-012.aRetenir: Failed LV lead: conduction system pacing as a bailout (2025 ESC consensus); LBBAP often preferred to His bundle pacing.
